"'''A Thousand Miles'''" (originally titled "'''Interlude'''") is song by American [[Pop music|pop]] singer-songwriter [[Vanessa Carlton]], released as her debut single. Written by Carlton and produced by Curtis Schweitzer and [[Ron Fair]], the song was serviced to American radio in February 2002 by [[A&M Records]] as the lead [[Single (music)|single]] from Carlton's first studio album, ''[[Be Not Nobody]]'' (2002).

The song originated in a piano riff that Carlton wrote in 1998, titled "Interlude". She later recorded a demo tape of the full song, which reached Fair at A&M Records. Its production was reworked to include an orchestra section, and it was retitled "A Thousand Miles" at Fair's insistence. To promote the song, an accompanying music video was released, featuring Carlton playing the piano while it moves through Los Angeles. It was also featured in the films ''[[Legally Blonde (film)|Legally Blonde]]'' (2001) and ''[[White Chicks]]'' (2004). 

"A Thousand Miles" received critical acclaim, with reviewers praising Carlton's vocals and the song's composition. It was nominated for three [[Grammy Awards]] at the [[45th Annual Grammy Awards]], including [[Grammy Award for Record of the Year|Record of the Year]]. The song was commercially successful, becoming Carlton's biggest hit in the United States and her only single to reach the top 10 of the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]], peaking at number five. It also reached number one in Australia, number three in Ireland, and the top 10 in the United Kingdom, France, Italy, the Netherlands, and New Zealand.

sections.heading: Background and recording
sections.wikitext:
[[Vanessa Carlton]] wrote the song's piano [[riff]] in mid-1998 at her parents' house in [[Philadelphia]]; her mother Heidi Lee, who had been listening to her, said, "Vanessa, that's a hit song."<ref name="VH1 interview">Stas, Heather. [http://www.vh1.com/news/articles/1453927/05132002/carlton_vanessa.jhtml "Vanessa Carlton: It's Not Easy Being Not Nobody"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071001063243/http://www.vh1.com/news/articles/1453927/05132002/carlton_vanessa.jhtml|date=October 1, 2007}}. [[VH1]]. May 13, 2002. Retrieved May 28, 2006.</ref> Carlton was unable to finish the song because of a case of [[writer's block]] and did not return to it for several months. While looking for a record label that would sign her, Carlton played the beginning of the song for a record producer, who said, "You have to finish that."<ref name="MTV Road to the Grammys">{{cite news |last1=Moss |first1=Corey |date=February 14, 2003 |title=Road To The Grammys: The Making Of Vanessa Carlton's 'A Thousand Miles' |url=http://www.mtv.com/news/articles/1469962/20030214/story.jhtml |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040308062236/http://www.mtv.com/news/articles/1469962/20030214/story.jhtml |archive-date=March 8, 2004 |access-date=March 1, 2023 |work=MTV News}}</ref> She returned to her parents' home and finished it in an hour one evening, naming it "Interlude." She told [[VH1]] in 2004, "I just sit down and write my songs ... It just kind of happened and it will never happen again like that."<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20050225160456/http://www.vh1.com/artists/interview/1495066/12202004/carlton_vanessa.jhtml "Vanessa Carlton: Cast Your Fate To The Wind"]. [[VH1]]. December 20, 2004. Retrieved June 28, 2006.</ref> 

Some years later, Carlton recorded a [[demo tape]] (which featured several tracks, including "Interlude") and sent it to various producers and labels in the hopes that one would sign her. Some expressed interest, but Carlton did not agree with their suggestions for alternative titles for the song. One of the tapes found its way to [[Ron Fair]], head of [[A&M Records]], who recalled that "It was extraordinary, but also in some respects kind of screwed up as a record. It didn't press the emotional buttons the way I envisioned it."<ref name="MTV Road to the Grammys" /> Carlton then met with Fair for a piano session to alter the arrangement of the song "so the heartbeat came in a different way". During this session, more transitions were inserted into the song, and the timing of the repetition of the chorus was changed. Additionally, the instrumental opening was shortened and an orchestra section was added by Fair; the lyrics, however, remained the same. He explained: "It has a lot of starts and stops to it, which makes it hard to achieve a flow, but I wanted to make a really dramatic record. The song is like a mini musical of its own."<ref name="MTV Road to the Grammys" /> 

"A Thousand Miles" took 14 sessions to record and was the first song recorded for ''[[Be Not Nobody]]''. As well as conducting the orchestra, Fair also organized a small band for its recording: John Goux played guitar on the track, [[Leland Sklar]] played [[bass guitar]], and [[Abe Laboriel, Jr.]] played drums. Carlton later said, "after listening to it I realized I was going to make an album that I was very proud of."<ref name="MTV Road to the Grammys" />

Carlton was unable to finish the song because of a case of writer's block and did not return to it for several months. While looking for a record label that would sign her, Carlton played the beginning of the song for a record producer, who said, "You have to finish that." She returned to her parents' home and finished it in an hour one evening, naming it "Interlude." She told VH1 in 2004, "I just sit down and write my songs ... It just kind of happened and it will never happen again like that." 

Some years later, Carlton recorded a demo tape (which featured several tracks, including "Interlude") and sent it to various producers and labels in the hopes that one would sign her. Some expressed interest, but Carlton did not agree with their suggestions for alternative titles for the song. One of the tapes found its way to Ron Fair, head of A&M Records, who recalled that "It was extraordinary, but also in some respects kind of screwed up as a record. It didn't press the emotional buttons the way I envisioned it." Carlton then met with Fair for a piano session to alter the arrangement of the song "so the heartbeat came in a different way". During this session, more transitions were inserted into the song, and the timing of the repetition of the chorus was changed. Additionally, the instrumental opening was shortened and an orchestra section was added by Fair; the lyrics, however, remained the same. He explained: "It has a lot of starts and stops to it, which makes it hard to achieve a flow, but I wanted to make a really dramatic record. The song is like a mini musical of its own." 

"A Thousand Miles" took 14 sessions to record and was the first song recorded for Be Not Nobody. As well as conducting the orchestra, Fair also organized a small band for its recording: John Goux played guitar on the track, Leland Sklar played bass guitar, and Abe Laboriel, Jr. played drums. Carlton later said, "after listening to it I realized I was going to make an album that I was very proud of."

sections.wikitext:
{{Listen

"A Thousand Miles" is written in the key of [[B major]] and composed with a [[tempo]] of 95 beats per minute.<ref>{{Cite web |title=BPM and key for A Thousand Miles by Vanessa Carlton {{!}} Tempo for A Thousand Miles |url=https://songbpm.com/@vanessa-carlton/a-thousand-miles |access-date=November 11, 2022 |website=Song BPM |language=en}}</ref> Carlton says that the song was inspired by a crush she had on a [[Juilliard School|Juilliard]] student (who is now a "very famous actor") whom she met while she was attending the [[School of American Ballet]].<ref name="MTV Road to the Grammys" /><ref name="Ghostarchive">Archived at [https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211205/GLO_57IV6Zc Ghostarchive]{{cbignore}} and the [https://web.archive.org/web/20210411151118/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GLO_57IV6Zc Wayback Machine]{{cbignore}}: {{cite web |date=April 11, 2021 |title=The Story of "A Thousand Miles" by Vanessa Carlton |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GLO_57IV6Zc&t=241s |website=[[YouTube]]}}{{cbignore}}</ref> She further stated that because she never actually spoke to her crush due to her shyness, she felt like she had "a better chance of falling up than ever having a relationship with this person".<ref name="Ghostarchive" /> She has also called the song "a combination of reality and fantasy. It's about a love that so consumes you that you do anything for it. That's how I felt at that time."<ref name="VH1 interview" />

The selection of the song's title was accompanied by a minor disagreement between Carlton and Fair, who was reportedly "adamant" about changing it. Fair said, "Vanessa Carlton is an incredible talent, but she's also very stubborn... I had to say, 'Look, I'm the president of the label, we're not calling it "Interlude". ' When you're trying to launch a career, people need a handle to pick things up from, and the word 'Interlude' is never in the song".<ref name="MTV Road to the Grammys" /> The final title of the song, "A Thousand Miles", was based on a suggestion by Fair's nephew. After the song's completion, Fair said that he listened to it repeatedly and "it made me weep. That's usually my litmus test. If I cry, I know it's a hit".<ref name="MTV Road to the Grammys" /> Despite this, he was concerned that the song's piano basis would put it at a disadvantage in the marketplace if it were to be released as a single.

She further stated that because she never actually spoke to her crush due to her shyness, she felt like she had "a better chance of falling up than ever having a relationship with this person". She has also called the song "a combination of reality and fantasy. It's about a love that so consumes you that you do anything for it. That's how I felt at that time."

The selection of the song's title was accompanied by a minor disagreement between Carlton and Fair, who was reportedly "adamant" about changing it. Fair said, "Vanessa Carlton is an incredible talent, but she's also very stubborn... I had to say, 'Look, I'm the president of the label, we're not calling it "Interlude". ' When you're trying to launch a career, people need a handle to pick things up from, and the word 'Interlude' is never in the song". The final title of the song, "A Thousand Miles", was based on a suggestion by Fair's nephew. After the song's completion, Fair said that he listened to it repeatedly and "it made me weep. That's usually my litmus test. If I cry, I know it's a hit". Despite this, he was concerned that the song's piano basis would put it at a disadvantage in the marketplace if it were to be released as a single.

sections.heading: Critical reception
sections.wikitext:
"A Thousand Miles" was highly acclaimed by music critics. ''[[Billboard magazine|Billboard]]'' magazine opined, "it's the song's classical-tied piano hook that endures with urgency throughout the song that lends it spectacular charm, along with the artist's vulnerable vocal style... A truly auspicious opening."<ref>Taylor, Chuck. [https://www.billboard.com/articles/news/76468/a-thousand-miles "Vanessa Carlton: 'A Thousand Miles'] ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]''. March 23, 2002. Retrieved March 19, 2006.</ref> Most other critics gave ''Be Not Nobody'' mixed reviews but generally praised the song. [[AllMusic]] wrote: "as it moves from its solo orchestral-backed choruses, the result isn't overwhelming, it's sweet, multi-layered, and appealing".<ref>Erlewine, Stephen Thomas. [{{AllMusic|class=album|id=r587920/review|pure_url=yes}} "''Be Not Nobody''"]. [[AllMusic]]. Retrieved March 19, 2006.</ref> Sean Richardson of the ''[[Boston Phoenix]]'' made favorable comparisons between "A Thousand Miles" and [[Michelle Branch]]'s debut single "[[Everywhere (Michelle Branch song)|Everywhere]]", saying, "it's a good-natured reverie, with none of the troubled soul searching that characterizes the work of [[Tori Amos|Tori]] and [[Fiona Apple|Fiona]]. She occasionally evokes her piano-playing predecessors by raising her girlish voice to a howl, but she's better off being herself".<ref>Richardson, Sean. [http://www.bostonphoenix.com/boston/music/other_stories/documents/02266748.htm "DIY divas: Michelle Branch and Vanessa Carlton"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120315062403/http://www.bostonphoenix.com/boston/music/other_stories/documents/02266748.htm |date=March 15, 2012 }}. ''[[Boston Phoenix]]''. May 16–23, 2002. Retrieved May 28, 2006.</ref> Adrien Begrand of ''[[PopMatters]]'' magazine said the song was "catchy and hard to dislike" but characterized it as "the sort of girly-voiced, introspective pop that is made to please people who are looking for singer/songwriters who look and sound profound, but actually have nothing to say".<ref>Begrand, Adrien. [http://www.popmatters.com/music/reviews/c/carltonvanessa-benot.shtml "Vanessa Carlton: ''Be Not Nobody''"]. ''[[PopMatters]]''. September 19, 2002. Retrieved March 19, 2006.</ref>

"A Thousand Miles" won in the Can't Get You Out of My Head category at the [[VH1]] Big in 2002 Awards,<ref>Moss, Corey. [https://web.archive.org/web/20021219192346/http://www.vh1.com/artists/news/1459010/12052002/run_dmc.jhtml "Run, DMC Break Down At VH1 Awards; Ice Cube, Vanessa Carlton Confused By Trophies"]. [[VH1]]. December 5, 2002. Retrieved May 28, 2006.</ref> and it was nominated for three [[Grammy Awards]]: [[Grammy Award for Record of the Year|Record of the Year]], [[Grammy Award for Song of the Year|Song of the Year]] and [[Grammy Award for Best Instrumental Arrangement Accompanying Vocalist(s)|Best Instrumental Arrangement Accompanying Vocalist(s)]] at the [[45th Annual Grammy Awards]]. It lost Song of the Year and Record of the Year to [[Norah Jones]]' "[[Don't Know Why]]", while the Best Instrumental Arrangement Accompanying Vocalist(s) award went to "Mean Old Man", performed by [[James Taylor]]. The song became popular amongst U.S. troops serving in [[Iraq War|Iraq]], and in April 2003, the ''[[Chicago Sun-Times]]'' reported that it had become the most requested song on the radio station [[British Forces Broadcasting Service]] Middle East. Carlton responded, "Perhaps, 'A Thousand Miles' conveys the feelings and longing and desperation that the U.S. soldiers feel for their loved ones. I don't know. But whatever peace I am able to bring to the hearts of the people at war is a contribution that I am proud of".<ref>{{cite news |last=Hermann |first=Andrew |title=Singer shoots to No. 1 with troops |date=April 6, 2003 |work=[[Chicago Sun-Times]] }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Roeper |first=Richard |author-link=Richard Roeper |title=Let's not tie patriotism to lame criminal ballad |date=April 9, 2003 |work=[[Chicago Sun-Times]] }}</ref> By May 2003 the website Musicnotes had sold a record 10,000 pieces of digital [[sheet music]] for "A Thousand Miles", and it won the website's Song of the Year award.<ref>[http://www.musicnotes.com/press/carltonaward.asp "Musicnotes, Inc. Presents Multi-Platinum Singer/Songwriter Vanessa Carlton With First Annual "Musicnotes Song of the Year Award""]. Musicnotes. May 6, 2003. Retrieved June 28, 2006.</ref> The song's production team was nominated for a 2003 Technical Excellence & Creativity Award in the category of Outstanding Creative Achievement in Record Production — Single or Track.<ref>[http://mixfoundation.org/tec/03nomineescreat.html "2003 Nominees: Outstanding Creative Achievement"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060720092811/http://www.mixfoundation.org/tec/03nomineescreat.html|date=July 20, 2006}}. Technical Excellence & Creativity Awards. Retrieved June 28, 2006.</ref>

"A Thousand Miles" was highly acclaimed by music critics. Billboard magazine opined, "it's the song's classical-tied piano hook that endures with urgency throughout the song that lends it spectacular charm, along with the artist's vulnerable vocal style... A truly auspicious opening." Most other critics gave Be Not Nobody mixed reviews but generally praised the song. AllMusic wrote: "as it moves from its solo orchestral-backed choruses, the result isn't overwhelming, it's sweet, multi-layered, and appealing". She occasionally evokes her piano-playing predecessors by raising her girlish voice to a howl, but she's better off being herself". sections.heading: Music video
sections.wikitext:
Fair played "A Thousand Miles" in front of his superior [[Jimmy Iovine]], the co-chairman of [[Interscope Geffen A&M Records|Interscope-Geffen-A&M]]. Iovine was very impressed with the song and requested that a [[music video]] be filmed immediately for it. After the video had been completed it was presented to Tom Calderone, the Vice President of Programming for [[MTV]], in early 2002. Calderone expressed a desire to begin broadcasting the video at once and Fair agreed to his request, even though the album was still in production at the time and Carlton's marketing "image" had not yet been developed.<ref name="MTV Road to the Grammys" />

Directed by [[Marc Klasfeld]], the music video was filmed in [[Newbury Park, California]], and in areas of [[Downtown Los Angeles]] such as [[State Theatre (Los Angeles)|State Theater]]. There was no use of [[Chroma key|green screen]] or visual effects; Carlton's piano and bench were moved using a flatbed truck and a custom-built dolly, and she wore a seat belt under her skirt to secure herself to the bench.<ref>Archived at [https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211205/GLO_57IV6Zc Ghostarchive]{{cbignore}} and the [https://web.archive.org/web/20210411151118/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GLO_57IV6Zc Wayback Machine]{{cbignore}}: {{cite web |date=April 11, 2021 |title=The Story of "A Thousand Miles" by Vanessa Carlton |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GLO_57IV6Zc&t=834s |website=[[YouTube]]}}{{cbignore}}</ref> 

Carlton told the website [[Contactmusic.com]] of the first time she watched the single's music video, in which she is seen playing the piano while traveling through a variety of settings:

{{blockquote|I was in the studio and had just taken a break, when someone ran in the room and said, "You're on MTV!" We put it on and I just stared at the screen. After a few minutes, I just covered my eyes and started to laugh. It seemed so surreal. The night after that, I heard the song on the radio for the first time. It was all so unbelievable.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20071015175516/http://www.contactmusic.com/new/artist.nsf/0/4d33044cc57edb6f80256eae003c68c9?opendocument&bio=full "Vanessa Carlton"]. ''ContactMusic''. Retrieved March 19, 2006.</ref>}}

Carlton felt that Klasfeld "captured who I was in that video",<ref name="VH1 interview" /> and he was selected to direct the video for the album's follow-up single, "[[Ordinary Day (Vanessa Carlton song)|Ordinary Day]]". The music video for "A Thousand Miles" received heavy airplay on the channel following its premiere on the top-ten video program ''[[Total Request Live]]'' on January 4, 2002, and was popular enough to be retired from the show's countdown.<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Wonsiewicz |first=Steve |date=March 8, 2002 |title=Pop Radio Supports Vanessa Carlton |magazine=[[Radio & Records]] |page=31 |issue=1443}}</ref><ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20060630042648/http://www.absolutetrl.net/records/records/retired.html "Retired Videos (1998—2003)"]. ''AbsoluteTRL.net''. Retrieved May 28, 2006.</ref>
sections.text:
Fair played "A Thousand Miles" in front of his superior Jimmy Iovine, the co-chairman of Interscope-Geffen-A&M. Iovine was very impressed with the song and requested that a music video be filmed immediately for it. After the video had been completed it was presented to Tom Calderone, the Vice President of Programming for MTV, in early 2002. Calderone expressed a desire to begin broadcasting the video at once and Fair agreed to his request, even though the album was still in production at the time and Carlton's marketing "image" had not yet been developed.

Directed by Marc Klasfeld, the music video was filmed in Newbury Park, California, and in areas of Downtown Los Angeles such as State Theater. There was no use of green screen or visual effects; Carlton's piano and bench were moved using a flatbed truck and a custom-built dolly, and she wore a seat belt under her skirt to secure herself to the bench. 

Carlton told the website Contactmusic.com of the first time she watched the single's music video, in which she is seen playing the piano while traveling through a variety of settings:

{{blockquote|I was in the studio and had just taken a break, when someone ran in the room and said, "You're on MTV!" We put it on and I just stared at the screen. After a few minutes, I just covered my eyes and started to laugh. It seemed so surreal. The night after that, I heard the song on the radio for the first time. It was all so unbelievable.}}

Carlton felt that Klasfeld "captured who I was in that video", and he was selected to direct the video for the album's follow-up single, "Ordinary Day". The music video for "A Thousand Miles" received heavy airplay on the channel following its premiere on the top-ten video program Total Request Live on January 4, 2002, and was popular enough to be retired from the show's countdown.

It continued to receive regular rotation on [[Adult contemporary music|adult contemporary]] and [[adult pop]] radio stations two years after its original release, and ''Billboard'' magazine has named it "one of the most enduring songs of the millennium".<ref>[http://www.rfnt.com/business_news_at_refernet/2004-08-15/Reviews.html "Billboard Single Reviews (Reuters)"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050214030052/http://rfnt.com/business_news_at_refernet/2004-08-15/Reviews.html|date=February 14, 2005}}. Retrieved May 28, 2006.</ref> Carlton has said that rappers such as [[Fabolous]] and [[Ja Rule]] "really like this song."<ref>{{cite web |date=June 9, 2002<!--, 14:21:02 (EDT)--> |title=Carlton Says Hip Hoppers Like 'Thousand Miles' |url=http://rapdirt.com/article1391.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030430032133/http://rapdirt.com/article1391.html |archive-date=April 30, 2003 |access-date=April 30, 2003 |work=RapDirt |quote=Vanessa Carlton tells The Atlanta Journal-Constitution while in town that some top hip hop stars are big fans of her breakout hit. "It must have some R&B vibe about it," she added.}}</ref> "A Thousand Miles" was [[sampling (music)|sampled]] in the [[Yungeen Ace]] single "[[Who I Smoke]]", a usage which Carlton approved of and defended from criticism.<ref>{{citeweb|url=https://hypebeast.com/2021/6/vanessa-carlton-defends-a-thousand-miles-sample-who-i-smoke|title=Vanessa Carlton Defends "A Thousand Miles" Sample on Rap Song "Who I Smoke"|publisher=[[Hypebeast (company)|Hypebeast]]|accessdate=May 15, 2026}}</ref>

sections.text:
"A Thousand Miles" is Carlton's most successful single and her only top-20 hit in the United States. It continued to receive regular rotation on adult contemporary and adult pop radio stations two years after its original release, and Billboard magazine has named it "one of the most enduring songs of the millennium". A writer for the Boston Phoenix said that with the song, Carlton "won favor with smart but awkward teenage girls who didn't see themselves in more evidently constructed teen-pop personalities like Britney Spears and Christina Aguilera", and Slant magazine said it "helped pave the way for an industry beginning to take a turn away from bubblegum pop". Carlton has said that rappers such as Fabolous and Ja Rule "really like this song." "A Thousand Miles" was sampled in the Yungeen Ace single "Who I Smoke", a usage which Carlton approved of and defended from criticism.

In its finished form, the song was first heard during a scene in the Reese Witherspoon film Legally Blonde (2001) and was included on the film's soundtrack under the title "A Thousand Miles (Interlude)". In the film White Chicks (2004), the song is used several times, including when Terry Crews' character sings along to it in a "perfect rendition".
